courses.title: Financial Accounting, BCom Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2024-25); university code COM-1.1

topics.title: Accounting concepts, conventions and standards
topics.summary: The basic assumptions and principles of accounting and the role of accounting standards.
notes: Accounting identifies, measures, records, classifies, summarises and communicates financial information.
Concepts: business entity, money measurement, going concern, accrual, dual aspect (Assets = Liabilities + Capital), consistency, matching, cost.
Conventions: conservatism (prudence), materiality, full disclosure, consistency.
In India, Ind AS (converged with IFRS) apply to listed and large companies; other entities follow the AS issued by the ICAI.
outcomes: Explain the main accounting concepts and conventions
State why accounting standards are needed

lesson.hook: A shop owner lends ₹10,000 of his own money to his shop. Is that the shop's money or his?

questions.q: Which concept says a business is separate from its owner?
Which convention says "anticipate no profit, provide for all losses"?

topics.title: Conversion of single entry into double entry
topics.summary: Finding profit by the statement of affairs method and converting incomplete records.
notes: Single entry is an incomplete system: usually only cash and personal accounts are kept.
Statement of affairs = Assets − Liabilities = Capital at a date.
Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital.
Missing figures (credit sales, credit purchases) are found from total debtors, total creditors and cash accounts.
outcomes: Find profit by the statement of affairs method
Prepare final accounts from incomplete records

lesson.example:
Opening capital ₹1,00,000, closing capital ₹1,40,000, drawings ₹20,000, additional capital ₹15,000.
Profit = 1,40,000 + 20,000 − 15,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹45,000.

questions.q: Why is drawings added back to closing capital?
questions.a: Drawings reduced capital but are not a loss, so they are added back to find the profit earned.

topics.title: Consignment and valuation of stock
topics.summary: Accounting by consignor and consignee, commission and the valuation of unsold stock.
notes: In a consignment the consignor sends goods to an agent (consignee) who sells them on commission; ownership stays with the consignor.
Pro forma invoice shows the goods' details; account sales is the consignee's statement of sales, expenses and commission.
Del credere commission is extra commission for bearing the risk of bad debts.
Unsold stock is valued at cost plus a proportion of non-recurring expenses (freight, insurance, carriage to the consignee's place); selling expenses are not added.
Normal loss is absorbed in the cost of the remaining goods; abnormal loss is credited to the consignment account and charged to profit and loss.
outcomes: Prepare the consignment account and consignee's account
Value closing stock with normal and abnormal losses

topics.title: Hire purchase accounting
topics.summary: Hire purchase and instalment purchase, interest calculation and journal entries.
notes: Under hire purchase the hirer gets possession at once but ownership passes only on payment of the last instalment.
Under an instalment sale, ownership passes at once.
Cash price = Total instalments − Total interest; interest is charged on the outstanding cash price.
The hirer records the asset at full cash price and charges depreciation on it.
outcomes: Calculate interest when the rate is given
Pass journal entries in the books of the hirer and vendor

lesson.example:
Cash price ₹30,000; down payment ₹6,000; balance in 3 annual instalments at 10% interest.
Year 1 interest = 10% × 24,000 = ₹2,400.

chapters.title: Accounting for Sale on Approval or Return and Royalty

topics.title: Sale or return
topics.summary: Recording goods sent on sale or return basis.
notes: Goods sent on approval are not a sale until the customer accepts them or the return period ends.
When few such transactions occur, entries are reversed at year end for goods not yet approved.
Unapproved goods are included in closing stock at cost (or net realisable value if lower).
outcomes: Record goods sent on sale or return
Adjust closing stock for unapproved goods

topics.title: Royalty accounts
topics.summary: Royalty, minimum rent, short workings and their recoupment.
notes: Royalty is payment to the owner of a right (mine, patent, copyright) based on output or sales.
Minimum rent (dead rent) is payable even if the royalty is lower.
Short working = Minimum rent − Actual royalty; it can be recouped from later excess royalty within the agreed period.
Short workings not recouped within the period are written off to profit and loss.
outcomes: Prepare the royalty analytical table
Pass entries in the lessee's books

courses.title: Corporate Law, BCom Semester 1
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2024-25); university code COM-1.2

topics.title: Company: meaning, features and kinds
topics.summary: Definition under the Companies Act, 2013, features and kinds of companies.
notes: Section 2(20) defines a company as one incorporated under this Act or any previous company law.
Features: separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, common seal (optional since 2015), transferable shares.
A private company needs at least 2 members (maximum 200) and 2 directors; a public company at least 7 members and 3 directors.
A one person company (section 2(62)) has one member; small companies and producer companies are other kinds.
outcomes: State the features of a company
Distinguish private, public and one person companies

topics.title: Incorporation, MOA and AOA
topics.summary: Promotion, incorporation, the memorandum and articles of association.
notes: A promoter conceives the idea and takes steps to form the company; pre-incorporation contracts do not bind the company unless adopted.
The memorandum (MOA) has clauses: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital and subscription.
The articles (AOA) are the internal rules; they are subordinate to the MOA and the Act.
Doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders dealing in good faith; constructive notice assumes they know the public documents.
Acts beyond the objects clause are ultra vires and void (Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche).
outcomes: Describe the stages of company formation
Distinguish MOA and AOA

topics.title: Prospectus
topics.summary: Meaning, contents and liability for misstatement.
notes: A prospectus (section 2(70)) invites the public to subscribe for securities.
A shelf prospectus is valid for one year; a red herring prospectus omits the price or quantity.
A statement in lieu of prospectus is filed by a company that does not invite the public.
Misstatement attracts civil liability (section 35) and criminal liability (section 34).
outcomes: Explain kinds of prospectus
State the liability for misstatement

topics.title: Directors
topics.summary: Appointment, qualifications, duties and kinds of directors.
notes: A public company needs at least 3 directors, a private company 2 and an OPC 1; the maximum is 15 unless a special resolution allows more.
Every director needs a DIN; at least one director must have stayed in India 182 days in the previous calendar year.
Listed public companies must have at least one-third independent directors (section 149).
Certain classes of companies must have at least one woman director.
outcomes: State the rules on number and appointment of directors
Explain the duties of directors

topics.title: Meetings and resolutions
topics.summary: Kinds of meetings, quorum, and ordinary and special resolutions.
notes: AGM (section 96): first within 9 months of the end of the first financial year; then within 6 months of year end, with no more than 15 months between two AGMs.
Quorum of a public company (section 103): 5 members if up to 1,000 members, 15 if 1,000–5,000, 30 above 5,000; private company: 2.
The board meets within 30 days of incorporation and at least four times a year, with no more than 120 days between meetings.
Ordinary resolution: votes for exceed votes against; special resolution: votes for are at least three times votes against.
outcomes: State the rules for convening meetings
Distinguish ordinary and special resolutions

topics.title: Winding up
topics.summary: Modes of winding up and the role of the liquidator.
notes: Under the Companies Act, 2013 a company is wound up by the Tribunal (NCLT); voluntary winding up is under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (section 59).
Grounds for winding up by the Tribunal include a special resolution, acts against sovereignty, fraud and failure to file accounts for five years.
The official liquidator or company liquidator realises the assets and pays creditors in the order of priority.
outcomes: Explain the modes of winding up
List the grounds for winding up by the Tribunal

topics.title: Nature and evolution of management
topics.summary: Meaning, functions and levels of management, and the classical theories.
notes: Management is getting things done through others by planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.
Levels: top (policy), middle (departmental), lower (supervisory).
F. W. Taylor's scientific management: time and motion study, differential piece rate, functional foremanship.
Henri Fayol gave 14 principles, including division of work, unity of command, scalar chain and esprit de corps.
outcomes: Describe the functions and levels of management
Compare Taylor's and Fayol's contributions

topics.title: Planning and decision making
topics.summary: Nature, types and steps of planning, MBO and decision making.
notes: Planning decides in advance what to do, how, when and by whom; it is the primary function.
Types of plans: objectives, strategies, policies, procedures, rules, programmes, budgets.
MBO (Peter Drucker): superior and subordinate jointly set objectives and review performance against them.
Decision making: identify the problem, develop alternatives, evaluate, choose, implement, follow up.
outcomes: Explain the steps in planning
Describe MBO

topics.title: Organisation structure
topics.summary: Departmentation, span of control, delegation and centralisation.
notes: Formal organisation is the deliberate structure; informal organisation arises from social relations.
Span of control is the number of subordinates one manager supervises effectively.
Delegation transfers authority, not ultimate responsibility; authority should match responsibility.
Structures: line, line and staff, functional, divisional, matrix.
outcomes: Draw and compare organisation structures
Explain delegation and decentralisation

topics.title: Motivation and leadership
topics.summary: Maslow's and Herzberg's theories and leadership styles.
notes: Maslow's hierarchy: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation needs.
Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (achievement, recognition) motivate.
McGregor's Theory X assumes people dislike work; Theory Y assumes they seek responsibility.
Leadership styles: autocratic, democratic (participative), laissez-faire.
outcomes: Apply motivation theories to workplace cases
Compare leadership styles

topics.title: Controlling
topics.summary: Steps in control and control techniques.
notes: Steps: set standards, measure performance, compare, take corrective action.
Management by exception: attend only to significant deviations.
Techniques: budgetary control, standard costing, ratio analysis, break-even analysis, PERT/CPM.
outcomes: State the steps in controlling
Relate planning and controlling

courses.title: Advanced Financial Accounting, BCom Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2024-25); university code COM-2.1

topics.title: Dependent branches
topics.summary: Debtors system and stock and debtors system for branches.
notes: A dependent branch keeps no full books; the head office records its transactions.
Under the debtors system, a branch account (nominal in nature) shows the branch's profit or loss.
When goods are invoiced at a price above cost, the loading is removed: loading = invoice price × mark-up ÷ (100 + mark-up).
Under the stock and debtors system separate branch stock, debtors, expenses and adjustment accounts are kept.
outcomes: Prepare a branch account under the debtors system
Remove loading from goods sent at invoice price

lesson.hook: A Bengaluru shop opens a branch in Mysuru. How does head office know whether the branch made money?
lesson.example: Goods sent at cost plus 25%; invoice price ₹1,00,000. Loading = 1,00,000 × 25 ÷ 125 = ₹20,000; cost ₹80,000.

questions.q: Goods invoiced at ₹60,000 at cost plus 20%. Find the loading.

topics.title: Departmental accounts and allocation of expenses
topics.summary: Trading and profit and loss accounts by department and the bases of apportionment.
notes: Departmental accounts show each department's results to judge its performance.
Common expenses are apportioned on suitable bases: rent by floor area, power by horsepower or units, advertising by sales, wages by hours or employees.
Inter-departmental transfers at a profit leave unrealised profit in closing stock, which is removed as a stock reserve.
outcomes: Apportion common expenses on fair bases
Prepare departmental trading and profit and loss accounts

topics.title: Claims for loss of stock
topics.summary: Estimating stock lost by fire and computing the claim with the average clause.
notes: Stock on the date of fire is estimated with a memorandum trading account using the normal gross profit ratio.
Stock lost = Estimated stock − Salvage.
Average clause: Claim = Loss of stock × (Policy value ÷ Value of stock on the date of fire), when the stock is under-insured.
Abnormal items (slow-moving stock) are dealt with separately at their own gross profit rate.
outcomes: Estimate stock destroyed by fire
Compute an insurance claim under the average clause

topics.title: Dissolution and the Garner v Murray rule
topics.summary: Realisation account, insolvency of a partner and the Garner v Murray decision.
notes: On dissolution, assets and outside liabilities go to the realisation account; profit or loss on realisation is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Order of settlement (section 48, Partnership Act, 1932): outside creditors, partners' loans, partners' capital, then any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio.
Garner v Murray: the solvent partners bear an insolvent partner's capital deficiency in the ratio of their capitals before dissolution, after making good their share of the realisation loss in cash.
outcomes: Close the books of a dissolved firm
Apply the Garner v Murray rule

topics.title: Piecemeal distribution
topics.summary: Paying partners as assets are realised, by the proportionate capital and maximum loss methods.
notes: Cash is applied first to realisation expenses and outside liabilities, then to partners.
Proportionate capital (surplus capital) method: pay first the partners whose capitals exceed their share in the profit ratio.
Maximum loss method: treat each instalment as if no more cash will come.
outcomes: Prepare a statement of piecemeal distribution
Compare the two methods

courses.title: Human Resource Management, BCom Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2024-25); university code COM-2.3

topics.title: Nature, scope and functions of HRM
topics.summary: Meaning, objectives and functions of HRM and the role of the HR manager.
notes: HRM is the management of people at work: acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining them.
Managerial functions: planning, organising, directing, controlling; operative functions: procurement, development, compensation, integration, maintenance.
HRM differs from personnel management by treating people as assets and linking HR to strategy.
outcomes: Explain the scope and functions of HRM
Distinguish HRM from personnel management

topics.title: HR planning, recruitment and selection
topics.summary: Human resource planning, sources of recruitment and the selection process.
notes: HR planning forecasts demand for and supply of employees and plans to close the gap.
Job analysis yields the job description (duties) and job specification (qualifications).
Recruitment sources: internal (promotion, transfer) and external (advertisement, campus, agencies, e-recruitment).
Selection steps: screening, tests, interviews, reference checks, medical examination, offer, induction.
outcomes: Describe the selection process
Compare internal and external recruitment

topics.title: Training methods
topics.summary: Need, methods and evaluation of training.
notes: Training improves skills for the present job; development prepares people for future roles.
On-the-job methods: job rotation, coaching, apprenticeship; off-the-job: lectures, case studies, role play, simulation.
Kirkpatrick's four levels of evaluation: reaction, learning, behaviour, results.
outcomes: Choose training methods for a need
Evaluate a training programme

topics.title: Performance appraisal and compensation
topics.summary: Methods of appraisal and components of pay.
notes: Traditional appraisal methods: ranking, paired comparison, graphic rating scale, checklist; modern: MBO, BARS, 360-degree feedback.
Common errors: halo effect, central tendency, leniency, recency bias.
Compensation includes basic pay, allowances (DA, HRA), incentives and fringe benefits.
outcomes: Compare appraisal methods
Identify rating errors

topics.title: Industrial relations and employee welfare
topics.summary: Grievances, discipline, trade unions and welfare measures.
notes: A grievance procedure resolves employee complaints in stages, from the supervisor upwards.
Collective bargaining is negotiation between employers and unions on terms of employment.
India's four labour codes (wages, industrial relations, social security, occupational safety) consolidate earlier labour laws.
outcomes: Describe the grievance procedure
Explain collective bargaining

courses.title: Quantitative Techniques for Business Decisions, BCom Semester 2
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2024-25); university code COM-2.4

topics.title: Ratios, percentages and interest
topics.summary: Ratio and proportion, percentages, simple and compound interest.
notes: Simple interest SI = PNR ÷ 100.
Compound amount A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ; with compounding k times a year, A = P(1 + r/(100k))^(nk).
Effective annual rate = (1 + r/(100k))^k − 1.
Percentage change = (New − Old) ÷ Old × 100.
outcomes: Compute simple and compound interest
Compare nominal and effective rates

lesson.hook: Is 12% a year compounded monthly the same as 12% compounded yearly?
lesson.example:
₹10,000 at 12% for 2 years. Yearly: 10,000 × 1.12² = ₹12,544.
Monthly: 10,000 × 1.01²⁴ ≈ ₹12,697. Monthly compounding earns ₹153 more.

questions.q: Find SI on ₹5,000 at 8% for 3 years.
What is the effective rate of 10% compounded half-yearly?

topics.title: Annuities
topics.summary: Present and future values of annuities and loan instalments (EMI).
notes: Future value of an ordinary annuity: A = P[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] ÷ i.
Present value of an ordinary annuity: V = P[1 − (1 + i)⁻ⁿ] ÷ i.
EMI = L × i(1 + i)ⁿ ÷ ((1 + i)ⁿ − 1), where i is the rate per period.
outcomes: Find the present and future value of an annuity
Compute an EMI

topics.title: Matrices in business
topics.summary: Matrix operations, determinants, inverse and solving equations.
notes: Matrices of compatible orders can be added and multiplied; AB ≠ BA in general.
A 2 × 2 determinant |a b; c d| = ad − bc.
A system AX = B with |A| ≠ 0 has the unique solution X = A⁻¹B; Cramer's rule gives x = Δx ÷ Δ.
outcomes: Solve simultaneous equations by matrices and Cramer's rule
Use matrices for cost and revenue problems

topics.title: Mean, median and mode
topics.summary: Averages of ungrouped and grouped data.
notes: Arithmetic mean of a frequency distribution: x̄ = Σfx ÷ N; by the step-deviation method x̄ = A + (Σfd′ ÷ N) × c.
Median = L + ((N/2 − cf) ÷ f) × c.
Mode = L + ((f₁ − f₀) ÷ (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × c.
Empirical relation: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
outcomes: Compute mean, median and mode of grouped data
Choose a suitable average

topics.title: Range, quartile deviation and standard deviation
topics.summary: Absolute and relative measures of dispersion.
notes: Range = L − S; coefficient of range = (L − S) ÷ (L + S).
Quartile deviation = (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ 2.
Standard deviation σ = √(Σf(x − x̄)² ÷ N).
Coefficient of variation = σ ÷ x̄ × 100; the series with the lower CV is more consistent.
outcomes: Compute standard deviation and CV
Compare the consistency of two series

courses.title: Corporate Accounting, BCom Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2025-26); university code COM-3.1

topics.title: Underwriting and underwriting commission
topics.summary: What underwriting is, its kinds, marked and unmarked applications, and the commission allowed by law.
notes: Underwriting is an agreement under which the underwriter undertakes to take up the shares or debentures not subscribed by the public, in return for a commission.

Complete underwriting covers the whole issue; partial underwriting covers part of it; firm underwriting means the underwriter also applies for a fixed number of shares regardless of public subscription.
Marked applications carry the stamp of a particular underwriter and are credited to that underwriter; unmarked applications are shared among underwriters in the ratio of their gross liability.

Under the Companies Act, 2013 (section 40) and its rules, underwriting commission may not exceed 5% of the issue price of shares or 2.5% of the issue price of debentures, or the rate authorised by the articles, whichever is less.
outcomes: Compute each underwriter's net liability with marked and unmarked applications
Calculate underwriting commission and pass the journal entries

lesson.hook: A company issues 1,00,000 shares but the public applies for only 80,000. Who buys the rest?

questions.q: What is the maximum underwriting commission on shares?
questions.a: 5% of the issue price, or the rate in the articles if lower.

topics.title: Methods of valuing goodwill
topics.summary: Average profit, super profit, capitalisation and annuity methods.
notes: Goodwill is the value of a firm's reputation and its ability to earn more than normal profits; it is an intangible asset.
Average profit method: Goodwill = Average maintainable profit × Number of years' purchase.
Super profit method: Normal profit = Capital employed × Normal rate of return ÷ 100; Super profit = Average maintainable profit − Normal profit; Goodwill = Super profit × Number of years' purchase.
Capitalisation of average profit: Capitalised value = Average profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return; Goodwill = Capitalised value − Net assets (capital employed).
Capitalisation of super profit: Goodwill = Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return.
Annuity method: Goodwill = Super profit × present value of an annuity of ₹1 for the given years at the given rate.
outcomes: Value goodwill by the average profit, super profit and capitalisation methods
Adjust past profits to find maintainable profit

lesson.hook: Two shops have identical stock and furniture, yet one sells for ₹5 lakh more. What is the buyer paying for?
lesson.example:
Capital employed ₹5,00,000; normal return 10%; average profit ₹70,000; 3 years' purchase.
Normal profit = ₹50,000; super profit = ₹20,000; goodwill = 20,000 × 3 = ₹60,000.
Capitalising super profit: 20,000 × 100 ÷ 10 = ₹2,00,000.

questions.q: Average profit ₹40,000, 4 years' purchase. Goodwill by the average profit method?
Why are abnormal gains removed from past profits?
questions.a: Goodwill depends on maintainable (future) profit, and abnormal gains will not recur.

lesson.homework: Value goodwill by all four methods for the data in the class example with an annuity factor of 2.4869 (3 years at 10%).

topics.title: Net assets, yield and fair value methods
topics.summary: Intrinsic (net assets) value, yield value and fair value of equity shares.
notes: Net assets (intrinsic value) method: Value per equity share = Net assets available to equity shareholders ÷ Number of equity shares.

Net assets available to equity shareholders = Total assets at realisable value (including goodwill) − Outside liabilities − Preference share capital (and any preference dividend in arrears where applicable).
Yield method: Value per share = (Expected rate of return ÷ Normal rate of return) × Paid-up value per share.
Fair value = (Intrinsic value + Yield value) ÷ 2.
outcomes: Value equity shares by the net assets and yield methods
Find the fair value of a share

questions.q: Expected return 15%, normal return 10%, paid-up value ₹100. Yield value?

topics.title: Schedule III formats
topics.summary: Preparing the statement of profit and loss and the balance sheet in the Schedule III format.
notes: Company financial statements follow Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013.
The balance sheet has two parts: Equity and Liabilities (shareholders' funds, non-current liabilities, current liabilities) and Assets (non-current assets, current assets).
Details are given in notes to accounts, which are referred to by number on the face of the statements.
Managerial remuneration of a public company may not exceed 11% of net profit (section 197) without approval in general meeting.
outcomes: Prepare a company's statement of profit and loss and balance sheet with notes
Classify items as current and non-current

courses.title: Financial Management, BCom Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2025-26); university code COM-3.2

topics.title: Objectives and functions of finance
topics.summary: Finance functions, profit versus wealth maximisation and the finance manager's role.
notes: Three finance decisions: investment, financing and dividend (plus liquidity).
Wealth maximisation (maximising the market value of shares) is preferred to profit maximisation because it considers time value and risk.
Agency problem: managers may pursue their own goals rather than shareholders'.
outcomes: Explain the three finance decisions
Compare profit and wealth maximisation

topics.title: Time value of money
topics.summary: Compounding and discounting, and the present value of annuities.
notes: Future value FV = PV(1 + r)ⁿ; present value PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ.
A rupee today is worth more than a rupee tomorrow because it can be invested.
PV of an annuity = A × [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] ÷ r.
Rule of 72: money doubles in about 72 ÷ r years.
outcomes: Compute present and future values
Value an annuity

lesson.hook: Would you take ₹1,00,000 today or ₹1,10,000 a year from now?
lesson.example: PV of ₹1,10,000 in one year at 12% = 1,10,000 ÷ 1.12 = ₹98,214, which is less than ₹1,00,000: take the money today.

questions.q: How long does money take to double at 8%?

topics.title: Capital budgeting techniques
topics.summary: Payback, ARR, NPV, IRR and profitability index.
notes: Payback period = Initial investment ÷ Annual cash inflow (for even cash flows).
ARR = Average annual profit after tax ÷ Average investment × 100.
NPV = PV of cash inflows − Initial outlay; accept if NPV > 0.
IRR is the rate at which NPV = 0; accept if IRR exceeds the cost of capital.
Profitability index = PV of inflows ÷ Initial outlay; accept if PI > 1.
outcomes: Evaluate projects with NPV, IRR, payback and PI
Explain why NPV is preferred

lesson.example:
Outlay ₹1,00,000; inflows ₹40,000 a year for 3 years; cost of capital 10%.
PV = 40,000 × 2.487 = ₹99,480; NPV = −₹520: reject. Payback = 2.5 years.

questions.q: A project's IRR is 14% and cost of capital 12%. Accept?
questions.a: Yes: IRR exceeds the cost of capital.

chapters.title: Cost of Capital and Capital Structure

topics.title: Cost of capital
topics.summary: Cost of debt, preference and equity, and the weighted average cost of capital.
notes: After-tax cost of debt Kd = I(1 − t) ÷ Net proceeds.
Cost of preference capital Kp = Preference dividend ÷ Net proceeds.
Cost of equity (dividend growth model) Ke = D₁ ÷ P₀ + g.
WACC = Σ(weight × cost of each source).
outcomes: Compute specific costs and WACC
Explain why debt is the cheapest source

topics.title: Leverage and capital structure
topics.summary: Operating, financial and combined leverage, and EBIT–EPS analysis.
notes: Operating leverage = Contribution ÷ EBIT; financial leverage = EBIT ÷ EBT; combined leverage = Contribution ÷ EBT.
EPS = (EBIT − Interest)(1 − t) ÷ Number of equity shares.
Trading on equity: using debt raises EPS when the return on investment exceeds the interest rate.
Capital structure theories: net income, net operating income, traditional, Modigliani–Miller.
outcomes: Compute leverages
Choose a financing plan by EBIT–EPS analysis

topics.title: Dividend policy and working capital
topics.summary: Dividend theories and working capital management.
notes: Walter's model: P = (D + (r/k)(E − D)) ÷ k; if r > k, retaining profits raises the share price.
Gordon's model: P = E(1 − b) ÷ (k − br); MM hold that dividend policy is irrelevant in perfect markets.
Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities; operating cycle = raw material + WIP + finished goods + debtors periods − creditors period.
outcomes: Apply Walter's and Gordon's models
Estimate working capital requirements

courses.title: Cost Accounting, BCom Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2025-26); university code COM-3.3

chapters.title: Introduction to Cost Accounting and the Cost Sheet

topics.title: Cost concepts and the cost sheet
topics.summary: Elements of cost, classification and preparing a cost sheet.
notes: Elements of cost: materials, labour and expenses, each direct or indirect; indirect ones form overheads.
Prime cost = Direct materials + Direct labour + Direct expenses.
Works (factory) cost = Prime cost + Factory overheads (adjusted for opening and closing WIP).
Cost of production = Works cost + Office and administration overheads; Cost of sales = Cost of production + Opening − Closing finished goods + Selling and distribution overheads.
Profit = Sales − Cost of sales.
outcomes: Classify costs by element, behaviour and function
Prepare a cost sheet and a quotation

lesson.hook: A bakery sells a cake for ₹500. How does it know whether that price covers flour, wages, rent and delivery?
lesson.example:
Materials ₹40,000, labour ₹25,000, direct expenses ₹5,000: prime cost ₹70,000.
Factory overheads ₹14,000: works cost ₹84,000. Office overheads ₹6,000: cost of production ₹90,000.
Selling overheads ₹10,000: cost of sales ₹1,00,000. Sales ₹1,20,000: profit ₹20,000.

questions.q: What is added to prime cost to get works cost?
questions.a: Factory (works) overheads, adjusted for work in progress.

topics.title: Stock levels and EOQ
topics.summary: Economic order quantity and the reorder, minimum and maximum stock levels.
notes: Economic order quantity: EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C), where A is annual consumption in units, O the cost of placing one order and C the carrying cost per unit per year.
Reorder level = Maximum consumption × Maximum reorder period.
Minimum level = Reorder level − (Normal consumption × Normal reorder period).
Maximum level = Reorder level + Reorder quantity − (Minimum consumption × Minimum reorder period).
Average stock level = (Minimum level + Maximum level) ÷ 2, or Minimum level + ½ Reorder quantity.
outcomes: Calculate EOQ and stock levels
Explain the ABC and VED techniques of inventory control

questions.q: Maximum consumption 500 units a week, maximum reorder period 6 weeks. Reorder level?

topics.title: Pricing of material issues
topics.summary: FIFO, LIFO, simple and weighted average methods.
notes: FIFO issues the earliest prices first; closing stock is at recent prices.
Weighted average price = Total cost of stock ÷ Total units, recomputed after each receipt.
LIFO is not permitted under AS 2 / Ind AS 2 for financial statements but may be studied for costing.
outcomes: Prepare a stores ledger under FIFO and weighted average
Compare the effect of pricing methods on profit

topics.title: Incentive plans
topics.summary: Time rate, piece rate and the Halsey and Rowan premium plans.
notes: Time saved = Time allowed − Time taken.
Halsey plan: Bonus = 50% × Time saved × Rate per hour; Earnings = Time taken × Rate + Bonus.
Rowan plan: Bonus = (Time taken ÷ Time allowed) × Time saved × Rate per hour; Earnings = Time taken × Rate + Bonus.
Taylor's differential piece rate pays a lower rate below standard output and a higher rate at or above it.
outcomes: Compute earnings under Halsey and Rowan plans
Compare incentive plans for worker and employer

topics.title: Labour turnover
topics.summary: Measuring and controlling labour turnover.
notes: Separation method: Number separated ÷ Average number of workers × 100.
Replacement method: Number replaced ÷ Average number of workers × 100.
Flux method: (Separations + Replacements) ÷ Average number × 100.
outcomes: Compute labour turnover rates
Suggest ways to reduce labour turnover

topics.title: Allocation, apportionment and absorption
topics.summary: Distributing overheads to departments and absorbing them into products.
notes: Allocation charges a whole overhead to one cost centre; apportionment shares it on a fair basis (rent by area, power by horsepower-hours).
Secondary distribution reallocates service department costs to production departments: direct, step or repeated distribution (or simultaneous equations).
Machine hour rate = Machine overheads ÷ Machine hours; labour hour rate = Overheads ÷ Labour hours.
Under-absorption or over-absorption is the difference between overheads absorbed and actually incurred.
outcomes: Prepare a primary and secondary distribution summary
Compute a machine hour rate

topics.title: Marginal costing and break-even analysis
topics.summary: Contribution, P/V ratio, break-even point and margin of safety.
notes: Contribution = Sales − Variable cost.
P/V ratio = Contribution ÷ Sales × 100.
Break-even point (units) = Fixed cost ÷ Contribution per unit; break-even sales (₹) = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio.
Margin of safety = Actual sales − Break-even sales; also Profit ÷ P/V ratio.
outcomes: Find the break-even point and margin of safety
Find the sales needed for a target profit

lesson.hook: A food truck pays ₹30,000 a month in fixed costs. How many plates must it sell before it makes a rupee?
lesson.example:
Price ₹100, variable cost ₹60, fixed cost ₹30,000. Contribution ₹40 a plate; P/V ratio 40%.
BEP = 30,000 ÷ 40 = 750 plates (₹75,000). For profit ₹10,000: (30,000 + 10,000) ÷ 40 = 1,000 plates.

questions.q: Sales ₹2,00,000, P/V ratio 25%, fixed cost ₹30,000. Find profit and margin of safety.

courses.title: Indian Financial System, BCom Semester 3
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024, 2025-26); university code COM-3.4

topics.title: Structure of the Indian financial system
topics.summary: Components and functions of a financial system.
notes: Components: financial institutions, financial markets, financial instruments and financial services, under regulators.
Functions: mobilising savings, allocating capital, providing payment systems, pricing and sharing risk.
Regulators: RBI (banking, money market), SEBI (securities), IRDAI (insurance), PFRDA (pensions).
outcomes: Describe the structure of the Indian financial system
Name the regulators and what they regulate

topics.title: Money market and capital market
topics.summary: Money market instruments, the primary and secondary capital markets, and stock exchanges.
notes: The money market deals in short-term funds (up to one year): call money, treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repos.
The capital market deals in long-term funds: the primary market issues new securities (IPO, FPO, rights, private placement); the secondary market trades existing ones.
India's main stock exchanges are the BSE (Sensex) and NSE (Nifty 50); trades settle on T+1.
Depositories NSDL and CDSL hold securities in demat form.
outcomes: Distinguish money market and capital market instruments
Explain how an IPO works

topics.title: RBI, banks and NBFCs
topics.summary: Functions of the Reserve Bank, commercial banks and non-banking financial companies.
notes: RBI functions: monetary authority, issuer of currency, banker to government, banker's bank, regulator of banks, manager of foreign exchange.
Monetary policy tools: repo rate, reverse repo / standing deposit facility, CRR, SLR, open market operations.
NBFCs lend and invest but cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques drawn on themselves.
outcomes: Explain the RBI's monetary policy tools
Distinguish banks and NBFCs

topics.title: Mutual funds, leasing and venture capital
topics.summary: Fund-based and fee-based financial services.
notes: A mutual fund pools investors' money; NAV = (Market value of assets − Liabilities) ÷ Units outstanding.
Fund types: open-ended and close-ended; equity, debt, hybrid, index funds and ETFs; SIPs invest a fixed sum regularly.
Leasing: a finance lease transfers substantially all risks and rewards; an operating lease does not.
Venture capital funds early-stage, high-risk businesses for equity.
outcomes: Compute a mutual fund's NAV
Compare fund-based and fee-based services

topics.title: Amalgamation and purchase consideration
topics.summary: Amalgamation in the nature of merger and of purchase (AS 14), and computing purchase consideration.
notes: AS 14: amalgamation in the nature of merger uses the pooling of interests method; in the nature of purchase uses the purchase method.
Purchase consideration by the net assets method = Assets taken over at agreed values − Liabilities taken over.
Net payment method: sum of payments in shares, securities and cash to the transferor's shareholders.
The transferor closes its books through a realisation account; the transferee records assets, liabilities and goodwill or capital reserve.
outcomes: Compute purchase consideration by the net assets and net payment methods
Pass entries in the books of transferor and transferee

topics.title: Capital reduction
topics.summary: Reducing share capital, writing off losses and the capital reduction account.
notes: Internal reconstruction reorganises a company's capital without forming a new company (section 66 needs Tribunal confirmation).
Capital is reduced by lowering the paid-up value or cancelling lost capital; the amount goes to the capital reduction account.
The capital reduction account is used to write off accumulated losses, fictitious assets and overvalued assets; any balance goes to capital reserve.
outcomes: Pass journal entries for capital reduction
Prepare the balance sheet after reconstruction

topics.title: Liquidator's final statement of account
topics.summary: Order of payment in liquidation and the liquidator's remuneration.
notes: Order of payment: secured creditors (to the extent of security), liquidation costs and liquidator's remuneration, preferential creditors, unsecured creditors, preference shareholders, equity shareholders.
Workmen's dues rank pari passu with secured creditors (section 326 overriding preferential payments).
Liquidator's remuneration is usually a percentage of assets realised and of amounts paid to unsecured creditors.
outcomes: Prepare a liquidator's final statement of account
Compute the liquidator's remuneration

topics.title: Consolidated balance sheet
topics.summary: Minority interest, cost of control and pre- and post-acquisition profits.
notes: A holding company controls a subsidiary (more than half the voting power or control of the board).
Minority (non-controlling) interest = Minority's share of share capital and reserves (both pre- and post-acquisition).
Pre-acquisition profits are capital profits and go to the cost of control; post-acquisition profits are revenue profits.
Cost of control (goodwill) = Cost of investment − (Holding's share of capital + pre-acquisition profits); a negative figure is capital reserve.
outcomes: Compute minority interest and cost of control
Prepare a consolidated balance sheet

topics.title: Correlation analysis
topics.summary: Scatter diagrams, Karl Pearson's coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation.
notes: Karl Pearson: r = Σdxdy ÷ √(Σdx² × Σdy²), with dx and dy deviations from the means; −1 ≤ r ≤ 1.
Spearman's rank correlation: R = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ (n(n² − 1)).
Probable error PE = 0.6745 × (1 − r²) ÷ √n; if |r| > 6 PE, correlation is significant.
Correlation does not imply causation.
outcomes: Compute Pearson's and Spearman's coefficients
Interpret the sign and size of r

lesson.hook: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together. Does ice cream cause drowning?
lesson.example: Ranks of 5 students by two judges give Σd² = 6. R = 1 − 6 × 6 ÷ (5 × 24) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

topics.title: Regression lines
topics.summary: Regression equations of y on x and x on y.
notes: y on x: y − ȳ = byx(x − x̄), byx = r σy ÷ σx; x on y: x − x̄ = bxy(y − ȳ), bxy = r σx ÷ σy.
r = ±√(byx × bxy), with the sign of the regression coefficients.
The two regression lines intersect at (x̄, ȳ).
outcomes: Fit regression equations and estimate values
Find r from regression coefficients

topics.title: Construction of index numbers
topics.summary: Simple and weighted index numbers and their tests.
notes: Laspeyres: P₀₁ = Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100; Paasche: Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100.
Fisher's ideal index = √(Laspeyres × Paasche); it satisfies the time reversal and factor reversal tests.
Cost of living index = Σ(I × W) ÷ ΣW (family budget method); real wage = Money wage ÷ CPI × 100.
outcomes: Construct Laspeyres, Paasche and Fisher indices
Compute real wages with a cost of living index

topics.title: Trend analysis
topics.summary: Components of a time series and measuring trend.
notes: Components: secular trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular variations.
Moving averages smooth fluctuations; use a period equal to the cycle length.
Least squares straight-line trend: y = a + bx, with a = Σy ÷ n and b = Σxy ÷ Σx² when x is measured from the middle year.
outcomes: Fit a straight-line trend by least squares
Compute moving averages

topics.title: Probability theory
topics.summary: Classical probability, addition and multiplication theorems.
notes: Classical probability P(A) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes.
Addition theorem: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
Multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B | A); for independent events P(A) × P(B).
outcomes: Solve probability problems with the addition and multiplication theorems
Distinguish mutually exclusive and independent events

courses.title: Costing Methods and Techniques, BCom Semester 4

topics.title: Contract costing
topics.summary: Contract accounts, work certified and profit on incomplete contracts.
notes: Contract costing applies to large jobs such as construction; each contract is a cost unit.
Notional profit = Value of work certified + Cost of work uncertified − Cost of work to date.
Profit to be credited on incomplete contracts: if 1/4 to 1/2 complete, 1/3 × notional profit × cash received ÷ work certified; if 1/2 or more, 2/3 × notional profit × cash received ÷ work certified.
Escalation clauses protect the contractor against price rises.
outcomes: Prepare a contract account
Compute profit on incomplete contracts

topics.title: Process accounts and losses
topics.summary: Normal and abnormal loss and gain in process accounts.
notes: Normal loss is unavoidable; its scrap value is credited to the process and its cost absorbed by good units.
Cost per unit = (Total cost − Scrap value of normal loss) ÷ (Input − Normal loss).
Abnormal loss is valued at the normal cost per unit and transferred out; abnormal gain likewise is debited to the process.
Equivalent production converts work in progress into completed units.
outcomes: Prepare process accounts with normal and abnormal loss
Compute equivalent production

lesson.example:
Input 1,000 units at ₹20,000; normal loss 10% (scrap ₹5 each); output 880 units.
Cost per unit = (20,000 − 500) ÷ 900 = ₹21.67. Abnormal loss 20 units = ₹433.

topics.title: Service costing
topics.summary: Cost units of services and transport costing.
notes: Operating costing finds the cost of services: transport, hotels, hospitals, power.
Composite units: passenger-km (transport), tonne-km (goods), room-days (hotels), bed-days (hospitals).
Costs are classed as standing (fixed), running (variable) and maintenance charges.
outcomes: Compute cost per passenger-km or tonne-km
Prepare an operating cost sheet

chapters.title: Reconciliation of Cost and Financial Accounts

topics.title: Reconciliation statement
topics.summary: Why cost and financial profits differ and how to reconcile them.
notes: Differences arise from items in financial accounts only (interest received, dividends, losses on sale of assets), items in cost accounts only (notional rent, notional interest), and different overhead absorption and stock valuation.
Start from cost profit and add or deduct each difference to reach financial profit (or the reverse).
Over-absorbed overheads are added to cost profit; under-absorbed overheads are deducted.
outcomes: Prepare a reconciliation statement
Explain the causes of difference

topics.title: Marketing concepts
topics.summary: Meaning of marketing and the evolution of marketing philosophies.
notes: Marketing creates, communicates and delivers value to customers and manages customer relationships.
Concepts: production, product, selling, marketing and societal marketing concept.
Needs, wants and demands: a want backed by purchasing power is demand.
outcomes: Distinguish the marketing philosophies
Explain needs, wants and demand

topics.title: Environment and buyer behaviour
topics.summary: Micro and macro environment and the consumer buying process.
notes: Micro environment: company, suppliers, intermediaries, customers, competitors, publics.
Macro environment (PESTLE): political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental.
Buying process: need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, post-purchase behaviour.
outcomes: Analyse a firm's marketing environment
Describe the consumer buying process

topics.title: STP
topics.summary: Bases of segmentation, target market strategies and positioning.
notes: Segmentation bases: geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural.
Targeting strategies: undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated, micro marketing.
Positioning places a product clearly in customers' minds relative to competitors.
outcomes: Segment a market for a product
Write a positioning statement

topics.title: Product and price
topics.summary: Product levels, the product life cycle and pricing methods.
notes: Product life cycle: introduction, growth, maturity, decline.
Branding, packaging and labelling add value and identity.
Pricing methods: cost-plus, competition-based, value-based; new product strategies: skimming and penetration.
outcomes: Relate marketing strategy to the PLC stage
Choose a pricing strategy

topics.title: Place and promotion
topics.summary: Distribution channels and the promotion mix.
notes: Channel levels: zero (direct), one (retailer), two (wholesaler and retailer), three (agent, wholesaler, retailer).
Promotion mix: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, direct and digital marketing.
AIDA model: attention, interest, desire, action.
outcomes: Design a distribution channel
Plan a promotion mix

topics.title: Digital and services marketing
topics.summary: Digital marketing channels and the extended marketing mix for services.
notes: Digital channels: search (SEO, SEM), social media, e-mail, content and influencer marketing.
Services are intangible, inseparable, variable and perishable.
Services marketing mix adds people, process and physical evidence (7 Ps).
outcomes: Explain the 7 Ps of services marketing
Compare digital marketing channels

courses.title: Income Tax Law and Practice I, BCom Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Basic concepts
topics.summary: Previous year, assessment year, person, assessee, income and the charge of tax.
notes: Income of the previous year (financial year) is taxed in the following assessment year (section 4).
Person (section 2(31)) includes an individual, HUF, company, firm, AOP/BOI, local authority and artificial juridical person.
Heads of income (section 14): salaries, house property, profits and gains of business or profession, capital gains, other sources.
Agricultural income (section 10(1)) is exempt but is used for rate purposes under partial integration.
outcomes: Explain the basic concepts of income tax
Name the five heads of income

topics.title: Residential status and incidence of tax
topics.summary: Resident, RNOR and non-resident individuals and the scope of total income.
notes: An individual is resident if in India 182 days or more in the previous year, or 60 days or more in the year and 365 days or more in the four preceding years (section 6).
The 60-day condition becomes 182 days for Indian citizens leaving for employment and for visiting Indian citizens or PIOs (120 days for those with Indian income above ₹15 lakh).
RNOR: non-resident in 9 of the 10 preceding years, or in India 729 days or less in the 7 preceding years.
A resident is taxed on world income; an RNOR and a non-resident only on income received or accruing in India (RNOR also on income from a business controlled in India).
outcomes: Determine an individual's residential status
Compute income taxable by residential status

lesson.hook: An Infosys engineer spends 200 days in the US this year. Does India tax her US salary?
lesson.example: In India 100 days this year and 400 days in the four preceding years: 60 + 365 days rule satisfied, so resident (unless an exception applies).

questions.q: In India 150 days this year and 300 days in the 4 preceding years. Resident?
questions.a: No: neither 182 days nor (60 days and 365 days) is met; non-resident.

topics.title: Salary, allowances and perquisites
topics.summary: Basis of charge, allowances, perquisites and deductions from salary.
notes: Salary is taxed on due or receipt basis, whichever is earlier (section 15).

HRA exemption (section 10(13A)) is the least of: HRA received; rent paid − 10% of salary; 50% of salary (Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Chennai) or 40% elsewhere; salary = basic + DA (forming part) + commission on turnover.
Standard deduction (section 16(ia)): ₹75,000 under the new regime (section 115BAC), ₹50,000 under the old regime.
Professional tax (section 16(iii)) is deductible under the old regime only.
outcomes: Compute income from salaries
Compute HRA exemption

questions.q: Under which regime is HRA exemption available?
questions.a: Only under the old regime; the new regime (section 115BAC) disallows it.

topics.title: Annual value and deductions
topics.summary: Gross and net annual value, standard deduction and interest on loan.
notes: Gross annual value is the higher of expected rent (municipal value or fair rent, limited to standard rent) and actual rent; unrealised rent and vacancy allowances apply.
Net annual value = GAV − Municipal taxes paid by the owner.
Standard deduction under section 24(a) is 30% of NAV; interest on borrowed capital is deductible under section 24(b).
For self-occupied property, annual value is nil; interest up to ₹2,00,000 is deductible under the old regime only.
outcomes: Compute income from house property for let-out and self-occupied houses
Apply the limits on interest deduction

topics.title: Rates of tax and rebate
topics.summary: Slab rates under the old and new regimes, rebate under section 87A and cess.
notes: New regime (section 115BAC, default) for AY 2026-27: nil up to ₹4 lakh; 5% to ₹8 lakh; 10% to ₹12 lakh; 15% to ₹16 lakh; 20% to ₹20 lakh; 25% to ₹24 lakh; 30% above.
Section 87A rebate under the new regime: full tax on total income up to ₹12 lakh (rebate up to ₹60,000); under the old regime up to ₹12,500 for income up to ₹5 lakh.
Old regime: nil to ₹2.5 lakh, 5% to ₹5 lakh, 20% to ₹10 lakh, 30% above (higher exemption limits for senior citizens).
Health and education cess is 4% of tax plus surcharge.
outcomes: Compute tax under both regimes
Decide which regime suits a taxpayer

courses.title: Management Accounting, BCom Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (NEP 2021 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Nature and scope of management accounting
topics.summary: Meaning, tools and limitations of management accounting.
notes: Management accounting provides information for planning, control and decision making.
Tools: financial statement analysis, ratio analysis, cash flow analysis, budgeting, standard costing, marginal costing.
Financial accounting serves outsiders and is governed by law; management accounting serves managers and is not.
outcomes: Distinguish financial, cost and management accounting
List the tools of management accounting

topics.title: Ratio analysis
topics.summary: Liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability ratios.
notes: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities (rule of thumb 2:1); quick ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities (1:1).
Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds.
Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold ÷ Average inventory; debtors' collection period = Average debtors ÷ Credit sales × 365.
Gross profit ratio = Gross profit ÷ Net sales × 100; return on capital employed = EBIT ÷ Capital employed × 100.
outcomes: Compute and interpret ratios
Prepare a balance sheet from given ratios

lesson.hook: A company's profit doubled, but it can't pay its suppliers. Which ratio would have warned you?
lesson.example:
Current assets ₹2,00,000 (stock ₹80,000); current liabilities ₹1,00,000.
Current ratio 2:1; quick ratio 1,20,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 1.2:1.

topics.title: Cash flow statement
topics.summary: Preparing a cash flow statement under AS 3 (indirect method).
notes: Cash flows are classified as operating, investing and financing activities.
Indirect method: start with net profit before tax, add non-cash and non-operating items, then adjust working capital changes.
An increase in current assets reduces cash; an increase in current liabilities increases it.
outcomes: Prepare a cash flow statement by the indirect method
Classify cash flows by activity

topics.title: Budgets and budgetary control
topics.summary: Functional, cash and flexible budgets.
notes: A budget is a quantitative plan for a future period; budgetary control compares actuals with it.
The key (limiting) factor decides which budget is prepared first, often sales.
A flexible budget shows costs at different activity levels, separating fixed, variable and semi-variable costs.
Zero-base budgeting justifies every expense afresh.
outcomes: Prepare cash and flexible budgets
Explain zero-base budgeting

topics.title: Variance analysis
topics.summary: Material and labour cost variances.
notes: Material cost variance = Standard cost of actual output − Actual cost = Price variance + Usage variance.
Material price variance = AQ(SP − AP); material usage variance = SP(SQ − AQ).
Labour rate variance = AH(SR − AR); labour efficiency variance = SR(SH − AH).
A positive (favourable) variance means actual cost was below standard.
outcomes: Compute material and labour variances
Interpret favourable and adverse variances

courses.title: Auditing and Assurance, BCom Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (NEP 2021 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Nature and types of audit
topics.summary: Meaning, objectives and kinds of audit.
notes: An audit is an independent examination of financial statements to express an opinion on whether they give a true and fair view.
Objectives: express an opinion (primary); detect and prevent errors and frauds (secondary).
Types: statutory, internal, government (CAG), tax audit (section 44AB); continuous, interim and final audits.
Standards on Auditing (SAs) are issued by the ICAI; SA 200 states the overall objectives.
outcomes: Explain the objectives of an audit
Distinguish statutory and internal audit

topics.title: Internal control, internal check and vouching
topics.summary: Internal control systems and vouching of transactions.
notes: Internal control comprises policies and procedures that safeguard assets and ensure reliable records.
Internal check divides work so that one person's work is automatically checked by another.
Vouching checks entries against documentary evidence (vouchers) for authority, accuracy and occurrence.
outcomes: Evaluate an internal control system
Vouch cash and credit transactions

topics.title: Verification of assets and liabilities
topics.summary: Existence, ownership, valuation and presentation of assets and liabilities.
notes: Verification establishes existence, ownership and title, valuation, and freedom from charge.
Inventories are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (AS 2).
External confirmations (SA 505) verify debtors and bank balances.
outcomes: Verify common assets and liabilities
Explain the auditor's duty about valuation

topics.title: The company auditor and the audit report
topics.summary: Appointment, qualifications, rights and duties of the company auditor; kinds of report.
notes: The first auditor is appointed by the board within 30 days of incorporation; later auditors at the AGM for a five-year term (section 139).
Rotation for listed and specified companies: an individual auditor for one term of 5 years; a firm for two terms of 5 years.
Section 141 bars certain persons (employees, debtors over ₹5 lakh, relatives holding securities) from appointment.
Opinions (SA 700, 705): unmodified, qualified, adverse, disclaimer; SA 706 adds emphasis of matter paragraphs.
outcomes: State the rules on appointment and rotation of auditors
Distinguish kinds of audit opinion

courses.title: Income Tax Law and Practice II, BCom Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

chapters.title: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession

topics.title: Computing business income
topics.summary: Admissible and inadmissible expenses and depreciation.
notes: Section 30–37 allow expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for business; personal and capital expenses are disallowed.
Cash payments over ₹10,000 to a person in a day are disallowed (section 40A(3)); excess payments to relatives (40A(2)).
Depreciation (section 32) is on the block of assets, written-down value; half rate if the asset is used for less than 180 days in the year of acquisition.
Presumptive taxation: section 44AD (8% of turnover, 6% for digital receipts), 44ADA (50% of professional receipts).
outcomes: Compute profits and gains of business
Compute depreciation on a block of assets

topics.title: Short-term and long-term capital gains
topics.summary: Capital assets, holding periods, computation and rates.
notes: Listed securities are long-term if held more than 12 months; other assets more than 24 months (from 23 July 2024).
Capital gain = Full value of consideration − (Cost of acquisition + Cost of improvement + Transfer expenses).

From 23 July 2024: STCG on listed equity (section 111A) 20%; LTCG on listed equity (section 112A) 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh; other LTCG 12.5% without indexation (land or building acquired before that date may choose 20% with indexation for resident individuals and HUFs).
Exemptions: section 54 (residential house), 54EC (specified bonds, up to ₹50 lakh), 54F.
outcomes: Compute short- and long-term capital gains
Apply exemptions under sections 54 and 54EC

chapters.title: Income from Other Sources and Clubbing

topics.title: Other sources and clubbing of income
topics.summary: Residuary income, gifts and clubbing provisions.
notes: Other sources include interest, dividends, family pension, casual income (taxed at 30% under section 115BB) and gifts.
Gifts from non-relatives exceeding ₹50,000 in a year are taxable (section 56(2)(x)).
Family pension: deduction of one-third or ₹25,000 (new regime) / ₹15,000 (old), whichever is less.
Clubbing: income of a minor child is clubbed with the parent's income (exemption ₹1,500 per child).
outcomes: Compute income from other sources
Apply clubbing provisions

topics.title: Deductions and computation of total income
topics.summary: Chapter VI-A deductions, set-off of losses and computing tax for individuals.
notes: Section 80C allows up to ₹1,50,000 (PF, PPF, life insurance, ELSS, tuition fees, principal on housing loan) under the old regime.
Section 80D: health insurance premium up to ₹25,000 (₹50,000 for senior citizens), more for parents.
The new regime allows few deductions (mainly 80CCD(2) employer's NPS contribution and 80CCH).
Losses: house property loss set off against other heads up to ₹2 lakh; business loss carried forward 8 years; long-term capital loss only against LTCG.
outcomes: Compute gross and net total income
Compute tax liability of an individual

courses.title: Goods and Services Tax, BCom Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (NEP 2021 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Concept and structure of GST
topics.summary: Indirect taxes before GST, the 101st Amendment and the dual GST model.
notes: GST was introduced on 1 July 2017 under the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016.
Dual GST: intra-state supply attracts CGST + SGST (or UTGST); inter-state supply and imports attract IGST.
The GST Council (Article 279A) recommends rates and rules.
GST is destination-based: tax goes to the state where goods or services are consumed.
outcomes: Explain the dual GST structure
Identify CGST, SGST and IGST transactions

topics.title: Supply, time and place of supply
topics.summary: Meaning of supply, composite and mixed supply, and the time and place of supply.
notes: Supply (section 7, CGST Act) includes sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal for consideration in the course of business.
A composite supply is taxed at the rate of its principal supply; a mixed supply at the highest rate among its items.
Place of supply decides whether a supply is intra-state or inter-state.
outcomes: Classify supplies as composite or mixed
Determine the place of supply in simple cases

topics.title: Registration and composition scheme
topics.summary: Threshold limits, compulsory registration and the composition levy.
notes: Threshold for registration: aggregate turnover ₹40 lakh for suppliers of goods only and ₹20 lakh for services (₹20 lakh and ₹10 lakh in special category states).
Inter-state taxable suppliers and e-commerce operators must register regardless of turnover.
Composition scheme: turnover up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in special category states); tax at a low rate on turnover, no input tax credit, no tax collected from customers.
GSTIN is a 15-character PAN-based number.
outcomes: State who must register
Decide whether the composition scheme suits a business

topics.title: Input tax credit
topics.summary: Conditions, blocked credits and utilisation of ITC.
notes: ITC conditions (section 16): tax invoice held, goods or services received, tax paid to government by the supplier, return filed, and the credit appearing in GSTR-2B.
Blocked credits (section 17(5)) include motor vehicles (with exceptions), food and beverages, club membership and goods for personal use.
IGST credit is used first for IGST, then CGST and SGST; CGST credit cannot pay SGST and vice versa.
outcomes: Compute ITC available
Set off ITC against output tax

lesson.example:
Output: CGST ₹50,000, SGST ₹50,000. ITC: CGST ₹30,000, SGST ₹30,000, IGST ₹20,000.
IGST 20,000 sets off CGST first: CGST payable 50,000 − 20,000 − 30,000 = 0; SGST payable 50,000 − 30,000 = ₹20,000.

topics.title: Returns, payment and e-way bill
topics.summary: Main GST returns, payment of tax and the e-way bill.
notes: GSTR-1: outward supplies (monthly or quarterly); GSTR-3B: summary return with tax payment; GSTR-9: annual return.
Tax is paid through the electronic cash ledger and electronic credit ledger.
An e-way bill is needed to move goods worth more than ₹50,000.
outcomes: Name the main returns and their purpose
Explain the e-way bill system
